report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **not simply false—it's context-dependent, and largely supported when conditions are favorable, but not universally true.**

**Evidence supporting a benefit:** Multiple controlled studies find that opening a bedroom window or internal door lowers CO2 buildup overnight, which correlates with better sleep. A DTU (Technical University of Denmark) study found that when ventilation kept CO2 below ~750 ppm, air quality was good enough that it did not impair sleep, and better ventilation was linked to improved next-day cognitive performance (dtu.dk). Related peer-reviewed work found that reducing ventilation (raising CO2 from ~856 to ~1,927 ppm) led to shorter deep sleep, more light sleep, and more awakenings (orbit.dtu.dk). A pilot study cited on ResearchGate found that opening a window (dropping CO2 from ~2,585 to ~660 ppm) significantly improved both sleep quality and perceived air freshness (researchgate.net). A 2023 MDPI study similarly links lower bedroom CO2 concentrations to better sleep quality (mdpi.com).

**Important caveats:** The Sleep Foundation reports on a Shanghai study where opening windows improved air quality but *not* overall sleep, because summer heat and outdoor noise entering through the open window offset the ventilation benefit (sleepfoundation.org). This shows the effect is not unconditional—outdoor noise, heat, cold, humidity, allergens, or pollution can counteract or reverse the benefit, particularly in polluted or noisy environments, or for people with asthma/allergies (aol.com, sciencedirect.com on air pollution/asthma).

**Bottom line:** The mechanism (lower CO2/better air exchange → better sleep) is well-supported by experimental data, but real-world benefit depends on outdoor conditions like temperature, noise, and pollution. So it's more accurate to say "usually true under good outdoor conditions" than outright false.
